top_story: Trump’s threat on 23 March to destroy Iran’s power infrastructure unless Tehran reopens the Strait of Hormuz pushed Tehran to signal a wider regional response, sharpening the Gulf’s exposure to rapid military escalation around a waterway that anchors energy flows and civilian livelihoods. That confrontation sits inside a longer US-centered security order in the Gulf that treats control of strategic access and deterrence of Iran as enduring priorities, sustaining a cycle in which coercive pressure invites broader regional risk rather than stability. Saudi Arabia’s passage of 2,000 executions under King Salman underscores how Gulf states are pairing external hard-power confrontation with intensified internal repression despite reform branding. The regional picture is one of governments hardening simultaneously across borders and at home, leaving societies more vulnerable to economic shock, fear, and narrowed political space.
